title: How the Framingham Heart Study Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Framingham Heart Study, the long-running Boston University-led cohort study launched in Framingham, Massachusetts after Truman signed the National Heart Act. They cover the rise of cardiovascular disease in the 1940s, FDR's fatal hypertension, the study's design and cohorts (original, Offspring, Omni, Gen Three, spousal), its major findings on smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, and physical activity, the Framingham Risk Score, criticisms about lack of diversity, and funding. The episode also includes tour announcements, banter about podcasts, diet and butter, and a listener mail segment correcting an earlier elephant seal episode.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce Gothic Theater and other tour dates, then riff on a mispronunciation of Framingham from an earlier episode and the growth of podcasts.

segments.title: Introduction to Framingham and the study
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Framingham, Massachusetts, a small Boston suburb known for the Framingham Heart Study, one of the most influential longitudinal studies in medicine, and mention the earlier tuberculosis study the town joined.

segments.title: Heart disease rise in the 1940s
segments.summary: Cardiovascular disease deaths rose in the mid-twentieth century as antibiotics and penicillin controlled infectious diseases, while little was known about preventing heart disease.

segments.title: FDR's hypertension and death
segments.summary: Roosevelt had high blood pressure that worsened, and he died in 1945 at age 63 after a stroke from hypertension, with a reading of around 300 over 190 noted; his death became a public catalyst for heart research.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break in the episode with off-topic conversation.

segments.title: Origins: National Heart Act and study design
segments.summary: Truman signed the National Heart Act, funding the study for twenty years. Gilson Metters described the mission to study coronary artery disease in an unselected population. Framingham was chosen for its middle-class, mid-sized, manageable population and its proven cooperation in the earlier tuberculosis study.

segments.title: Participants, diversity and cohorts
segments.summary: Participants aged 30 to 59 were recruited, initially through civic groups and word of mouth, which limited randomness. The population was predominantly white and male-focused at first, though women were included. Additional cohorts were added: Offspring, spouses, Omni, and Gen Three, with the study expanding to include more diverse groups.

segments.title: Major findings and the Framingham Risk Score
segments.summary: The study confirmed links between smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, menopause, physical activity, and cardiovascular disease, and coined the term risk factor. The Framingham Risk Score estimates ten-year heart disease risk using age, gender, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, and systolic blood pressure.

segments.title: Later research, funding and wrap-up
segments.summary: The study expanded into dementia, stress, sleep apnea, and brain donation research; other risk calculators were developed for women and minorities. Funding came from private donors and eventually Nixon's support. The hosts recommend further reading.
